This paper introduces a unified rating system that measures the relative difficulty of test samples and the performance of models. Initially, this paper received borderline reviews (1 borderline reject, 3 borderline accept). Reviewers appreciated the idea of rating the test sample difficulty (SVhy, e1WC, tj1B), the proposed rating framework (P3tp) and the diversity of the tasks investigated (e1WC, tj1B). However, reviewers had several concerns including the limited number of datasets and models tested (P3tp), the high correlation between the newly proposed metric and existing ones (tj1B), the dependence of the rating system of the quality of models involved in the evaluation (SVhy), the reliance on an oracle (e1WC), the new hyperparameters introduced in the proposed method (P3tp), the limited support for open-ended tasks (e1WC) and the lack of qualitative insights (e1WC).

After the rebuttal reviewers felt most of their concerns had been addressed, leading to final ratings of 3 accept, 1 borderline accept. The AC agrees with the reviewer assessment that this paper should be accepted and strongly encourages authors to include the clarifications made in the rebuttal in the final version.

Dear tj1B,

Please read the other reviews and the author response asap and let me and the authors know if you have any remaining concerns.

Particularly, were your concerns about the correlation with existing metrics, the use of "task mastery", and the distinction between hard examples and poor quality examples addressed by the rebuttal?

Best, AC

# Reviewer SVhY
## 1. Sensitivity to number of models
**One possible concern with the proposed method is that the effectiveness and outcomes of the rating system may heavily depend on the number and quality of model agents participating in the competition. If only a few models are used, the evaluation of sample-wise difficulty may be inaccurate, and the results could vary significantly depending on the number of participating models.**

**Ans:** Thank you for raising the concern regarding the potential sensitivity of AGI-Elo to the number and quality of participating models. We agree that the reliability of the rating system can be influenced by both the number and the strength of the models involved. 
To investigate this, we conducted additional ablation studies on the ImageNet dataset by systematically varying the number of evaluated models: $N_{\text{model}} = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30$. In addition to the 20 models described in Appendix B.1 of our paper, we incorporated 10 more models to form a pool of 30. For each setting, we randomly sampled subsets of models 100 times to vary the combinations of model strengths. We then computed the average Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients for test cases and models ($\bar{\rho}_t$, $\bar{\rho}_a$), as well as the mean absolute error (MAE) and mean squared error (MSE), to assess the stability and accuracy of our rating system. The results are summarized below:

| $N_{model}$ | $\bar{\rho}_t \downarrow$ | $\bar{\rho}_a \uparrow$ | avg. MAE $\downarrow$ | avg. MSE $\downarrow$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | -0.8894 | 0.9900 | 0.0792 | 0.0098 |
| 10 | -0.9307 | 1.0000 | 0.0593 | 0.0070 |
| 15 | -0.9526 | 0.9996 | 0.0526 | 0.0054 |
| 20 | -0.9674 | 0.9994 | 0.0475 | 0.0047 |
| 25 | -0.9740 | 0.9995 | 0.0439 | 0.0042 |
| 30 | -0.9792 | 0.9996 | 0.0420 | 0.0038 |

The changes in Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients show that model rankings remain highly stable regardless of the number of models, as reflected by the consistently high $\bar{\rho}_a$. In contrast, test case rankings show slightly more variability with smaller model sets, indicating that a larger pool of models improves the robustness of test case evaluation through a more reliable "crowd vote".

In terms of predictive accuracy, we can observe that as the number of participating models increase, the system becomes more accurate. From the trends in the two error metrics, we observe diminishing returns as the number of models increases. For instance, increasing $N_{\text{model}}$ from 5 to 10 reduces MAE and MSE by 0.0199 and 0.0028, respectively, whereas increasing from 25 to 30 yields only minor improvements (0.0019 in MAE and 0.0003 in MSE). 

In summary, while AGI-Elo produces stable model rankings even with a smaller number of models, both the stability of test case rankings and the overall accuracy benefit from a larger model population. For applications where predictive precision is critical, we recommend including as many diverse models as possible to ensure robust evaluation outcomes.

# Reviewer P3tp
## 1. Limited number of models and datasets per task
**The experiments are not really extensive. Specifically, the number of datasets and models is small, with only one per task.**

**Ans:** We acknowledge your valid point regarding the limited number of datasets and models per task. In our study, we prioritize evaluating a diverse range of tasks, which inherently introduces a practical trade-off between task diversity and the extensiveness of datasets and models evaluated. To mitigate this limitation, we have carefully selected representative, state-of-the-art datasets for each task, thereby ensuring the robustness and reliability of our conclusions. Furthermore, our additional analyses demonstrate that increasing the number of models per task leads to stable and consistent AGI-Elo rankings over time, further validating the effectiveness of our evaluation framework.

## 2. Hyperparameters: choices of initial rating values
**The proposed framework requires pre-defining some non-trivial hyperparameters such as the initial rating distribution and the rating bin.**

**In the experiment setup, the players (both agents and test cases) are initialized with a rating from a normal distribution with fixed mean and variance (i.e., $N(1500, 350^2)$), where do these numbers come from? How robust of your framework with different means and variances?**

**Ans:** Thank you for raising the question regarding our choice of hyperparameters. 
In fact, both the mean and variance of the initial rating distribution do not affect the final results of our system, as explained below:
- **Mean:** One of the beautiful properties of the Elo system is that the ratings are translation-invariant (as mentioned in Section 2.2 of our paper). Shifting all ratings by a constant value does not affect the expected outcome. Only the relative difference in ratings between the players determines the result, as the absolute scale is arbitrary and does not influence ranking behavior. For example, initializing the system with a rating of 1000 instead of 1500 would result in an exactly the same distribution situated 500 rating points left of the current graph, while their relative performances and expected outcomes remain exactly the same.
- **Variance:** As shown in Equations (6) and (7) in our paper, the variance reflects the uncertainty in a player's strength estimate. It will affect the magnitude of the rating change after each match. A larger variance leads to greater rating updates during early stages, allowing faster adaptation when little is known. However, this only affects the convergence speed, not the final ratings themselves. Once the ratings stabilize, the final outcomes are independent of the initial variance setting. 

Given that the choice of initial ratings would not distort the rating distributions, we adopted an initial rating of $\mathcal{N}(1500, 350^2)$ in order to follow the conventions used in modern chess rating systems. In this way, the rating values can be relatable to the existing Elo ratings of chess players of various strengths, making the ratings more intuitive to a broad audience familiar with Elo-style scores. 

## 3. Regression tasks
**It seems that the paper lacks a standard regression task. Can this framework extend to a regression task, such as evaluating monocular depth estimation in the vision domain?**

**Ans:** We thank you for your suggestion on how AGI-Elo could be extended to more types of tasks. In our paper, three out of six tasks we evaluated are regression tasks: object detection (bounding box regression), motion prediction (waypoint regression), and motion planning (waypoint regression). Thus, we believe that AGI-Elo is generally applicable to most regression tasks (including the monocular depth estimation) as long as scalar metrics are applied.

# Reviewer tj1B

## 1. Rank-reversal cases \& insights unattainable by conventional methods
**The experiments show that the model rankings produced by AGI-Elo are highly correlated with those from traditional aggregate metrics. This consistency weakens the argument for adopting such a complex framework. To better demonstrate its unique value, the authors should provide or discuss a "rank-reversal" case—where Model A has a higher average score but a lower Elo rating than Model B—to prove that AGI-Elo can offer insights unattainable by conventional methods.**

**Ans:** Thank you for this insightful suggestion. We do agree that demonstrating "rank-reversal" cases can indeed add value to AGI-Elo. In fact, in Table II of our paper, the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient $\rho_{a}$ on both ImageNet and LiveCodeBench is 0.9985, instead of perfectly 1, which indicates the existence of such "rank-reversal" cases in the model rankings. More specifically, on the ImageNet dataset, the "rank-reversal" case happened between ViT-B-16 (Acc. 0.81066, rating 1969.5) and Swin-T (Acc. 0.81088, rating 1969.0); while on the LiveCodeBench dataset, the "rank-reversal" case happened between GPT-4.1-mini (Acc. 0.77019, rating 1832.1) and o1-mini (Acc. 0.77361, rating 1820.5). Generally, we believe that such reversals are likely to occur when models have very close performance on a benchmark dataset. 

Meanwhile, besides providing new perspectives on model performances, our methods is also able to provide several insights that are unattainable by conventional evaluation metrics: 

- **Quantitative Estimation of Difficulty:** Our method is able to simultaneously estimate the difficulty of the test cases and their distributions in a dataset. We believe this fine-grained difficulty rating would provide lots of opportunities in applications such as dataset evaluation, model curriculum learning, etc. 
- **Performance Prediction:** One of the key properties of the Elo system is that it allows predicting how well the model will perform based on its score and the score of the test cases. For example, given a model with an estimated rating of 2000, and a test case of 1600 rating, we can expect that the model would achieve an accuracy of about 91% on this test case. This important property would allow us to efficiently evaluate and predict the performance of models without massive and repetitive testing. 
- **Task Mastery Level:** By analysing the difficulty distribution on datasets and leveraging the predictive power of the Elo system, AGI-Elo enables us to estimate the gaps between existing models and a certain desirable competency level. 

## 2. "Task mastery" on datasets vs. the real world

**Equating "task mastery" with conquering a specific dataset is a significant limitation and risks circular reasoning. "Task mastery" is defined by the ability to solve the hardest instance within the dataset, but this instance only represents the most difficult sample collected so far, not the full spectrum of real-world challenges. This conflation should be addressed.**

**Ans:** Thank you for highlighting that "task mastery" measured on datasets does not directly equate to real-world "task mastery". We agree with this observation and would like to clarify the following:

Firstly, it is true that no dataset can perfectly model the distribution in the real world. Thus, all performance evaluation methods operating on datasets would unavoidably share the same limitation as ours. However, we consider this an inherent challenge in dataset construction, yet it should not hinder the development of evaluation methods. The focus of our paper is to propose a novel evaluation method that is able to estimate the difficulty distribution and the “task mastery” on a collection of test cases. This has been successfully verified with our experiments.

Secondly, to clarify the definition of "task mastery", we are not simply equating the "task mastery" in the real world to the "task mastery" on a specific dataset or datasets. As discussed in Section 3.4 of our paper, we stated: "Assuming the dataset is a faithful miniature reflection of the real-world distribution of test cases, the oracle’s performance on the most difficult test case in the dataset serves as a proxy for its worst-case performance in the real world." Hence, we emphasize that the extension of dataset-based evaluation outcomes to real-world conditions relies on the critical assumption that datasets accurately mirror real-world task distributions. Only in the presence of the key assumption that the distribution of test cases in a dataset is faithful to that of the real world can we generalize the task mastery obtained from the datasets to the task mastery in the real world. 

Thirdly, datasets remain essential tools designed to be representative of real-world conditions, to train and evaluate models. Under the current conditions, these datasets are still the best medium for performance evaluation. While recognizing their inherent limitations, we also believe in the refinement of datasets. We do understand the limitations of existing datasets, that they may not accurately reflect the distributions in the real world. We believe that in a constant effort to approximate the real-world distribution more accurately, datasets can always be updated and include all newly observed test cases, to alleviate this limitation.


## 3. "Cognitively hard" vs. "data quality issue"?
**The AGI-Elo system cannot distinguish between what is "cognitively hard" and what is a "data quality issue." An instance that is mislabeled, blurry, or ambiguous will likely cause all models to fail, leading the system to assign it a very high difficulty rating. This is misleading, as it may direct research efforts toward fixing noisy data rather than solving genuine, complex challenges.**

**Ans:** Thank you for raising this important concern.

The objective of our work is to introduce a novel evaluation framework that quantitatively assesses the difficulty of individual test cases within a dataset, which is a unique capability among current evaluation methods. The notion of "difficulty" in this context can arise from a variety of sources and often reflects the complex interplay of multiple factors, making it challenging to provide an exhaustive enumeration of all contributing elements. 

Based on the sources of difficulties suggested by the reviewer, we think that they can be categorized into two different types:


- **Human-induced errors** such as inaccuracies in data collection, like mislabelling or ambiguous meaning (especially in ImageNet) are undesirable. Among all the difficult cases identified by our framework, these special cases can be efficiently addressed or removed through a manual inspection.
 
- **Inherent complexity**, including factors such as blurry (and similarly, occlusion, adverse weather, or challenging lighting conditions), represents realistic challenges that models are expected to handle in real-world applications. These challenges are both valid and essential for robust evaluation. However, in scenarios where a highly controlled or "clean" dataset is required, such samples can also be excluded subsequently.

Therefore, it is not our intention to mislead the research focus from addressing inherent task complexity toward merely identifying human-induced errors. We acknowledge that studying and understanding the inter-tangled mechanism between these two types of difficulties is a challenging problem. As a step in this direction, our method is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to quantitatively define and estimate the notion of "difficulty", and we believe this represents a significant advance toward tackling this broader challenge.

rebuttal.value:
# Reviewer e1WC

## 1. Support for open-ended tasks

**Limited support for open-ended tasks: AGI-Elo assumes that performance can be reduced to scalar scores, which may makes it less applicable to complex tasks like dialogue or free-form generation where evaluation is subjective or multi-dimensional.**

**Ans:** Thank you for raising this important point. We fully agree that extending the applicability of AGI-Elo to a broader range of tasks is a meaningful direction for future work. By design, AGI-Elo operates on scalar performance scores, and thus it inherently requires that task outputs be quantifiable. We acknowledge that this imposes limitations on its direct applicability to open-ended tasks such as dialogue or free-form text generation, where evaluation is often subjective or multi-dimensional. That said, free-form generation tasks can often be evaluated through established metrics that yield scalar values. These tasks typically fall into two broad categories:

- Reference-based evaluation, where outputs are compared to ground-truth answers. Metrics such as BLEU [1] (for language generation) or Fréchet Inception Distance (FID, for image generation) [2] are commonly used to quantify similarity between generated outputs and references. These scalar metrics can be directly incorporated into the AGI-Elo framework.
- Preference-based evaluation, often used in large language models (LLMs), where human annotators assign preference scores to outputs. More recently, automated evaluation via LLM-generated judgments or reward models has also gained traction. In such cases, the output of the evaluation process can again be reduced to scalar scores.
\end{itemize}
In summary, while AGI-Elo cannot directly operate on raw, non-scalar metrics, we believe that a secondary evaluation step can enable its application to many open-ended tasks. We view this as a promising area for future expansion of the framework.

## 2. Reliance on oracle models
**Oracle dependency: The framework relies on a fixed oracle model to define the mastery gap, but the paper does not rigorously justify or analyze the sensitivity of AGI-Elo to the oracle’s accuracy or definition.**

**Ans:** Thank you for pointing out this important clarification regarding oracle dependency. To clarify explicitly, our framework does not rely on any oracle model to define the mastery gap, nor do we employ such an oracle in our experiments.
The concept of an "oracle" presented in our paper serves solely as a theoretical reference point, illustrating where future models with higher skill levels might be positioned relative to current performance standards. The hypothetical oracles with different confidence levels and their ratings are in fact computed based on the distribution of the test cases in the post-experiment analysis. 
Thus, AGI-Elo’s evaluation does not depend on oracle accuracy or a particular oracle model definition. In fact, the oracles are determined by the rating distribution of the test case on a task.


## 3. Lack of qualitative insights
**Lack of qualitative insights: While the system produces interpretable scores, the paper does not explore case studies or failure modes that demonstrate what AGI-Elo reveals beyond traditional metrics.**

**Ans:** Thank you for your valuable suggestion regarding the need to provide more qualitative insights. To address this, we would like to highlight that qualitative examples supplementing our results have already been made publicly available on HuggingFace prior to our paper submission. From those qualitative examples, we can observe several insights by examining their difficulties estimated by AGI-Elo. For example, we conducted a case study on the most challenging test samples on two vision benchmark datasets, ImageNet and COCO, and found the following insights:

- **Image Classification (ImageNet):** Our analysis of the most difficult samples revealed several recurring patterns. Many challenging images lacked sufficient visual context due to aggressive cropping, making the object difficult to recognize even for humans. Additionally, images containing multiple semantically related classes (e.g., a crib with a baby, or a forklift near a car) often led models to prioritize the less prominent or contextually dominant object, resulting in misclassification. 
- **Object Detection (COCO):** For object detection, difficult cases commonly involved occlusion, where the target object was partially obscured and thus harder to detect. Another recurring theme was contextual deviation: for example, objects such as trucks were misidentified when situated in atypical backgrounds (e.g., a truck on a billboard rather than on a road), highlighting the model’s reliance on contextual priors.

These examples demonstrate that AGI-Elo not only provides interpretable scores, but is also effective in facilitating the identification of failure modes that are less accessible through aggregate metrics alone. We believe such insights are critical for understanding and improving model robustness in real-world applications.

### Reference

[1] Papineni, K., Roukos, S., Ward, T., \& Zhu, W. J. (2002). BLEU: A method for automatic evaluation of machine translation. Proceedings of the 40th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 311–318. https://doi.org/10.3115/1073083.1073135.

[2] Heusel, M., Ramsauer, H., Unterthiner, T., Nessler, B., \& Hochreiter, S. (2017). GANs Trained by a Two Time-Scale Update Rule Converge to a Local Nash Equilibrium. NeurIPS 2017.

Instead of relying on aggregate metrics, the method treats each model-instance interaction as a competitive match, generating a unified, probabilistic rating for both models and tasks on the same scale.

strengths_contributions.value:
The work moves beyond aggregate metrics by providing a fine-grained view of dataset difficulty, effectively highlighting the "long-tail" of challenging instances.

Extensive experiments across six established benchmarks demonstrate the framework's versatility.

The paper is exceptionally well-written and organized.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The experiments show that the model rankings produced by AGI-Elo are highly correlated with those from traditional aggregate metrics. This consistency weakens the argument for adopting such a complex framework. To better demonstrate its unique value, the authors should provide or discuss a "rank-reversal" case—where Model A has a higher average score but a lower Elo rating than Model B—to prove that AGI-Elo can offer insights unattainable by conventional methods.


Equating "task mastery" with conquering a specific dataset is a significant limitation and risks circular reasoning. "Task mastery" is defined by the ability to solve the hardest instance within the dataset, but this instance only represents the most difficult sample collected so far, not the full spectrum of real-world challenges. This conflation should be addressed.

The AGI-Elo system cannot distinguish between what is "cognitively hard" and what is a "data quality issue." An instance that is mislabeled, blurry, or ambiguous will likely cause all models to fail, leading the system to assign it a very high difficulty rating. **This is misleading, as it may direct research efforts toward fixing noisy data rather than solving genuine, complex challenges.**

summary.value: This paper proposes AGI-Elo, a unified, interpretable, and probabilistic rating system for evaluating the performance of AI models (or humans) on multimodal tasks, including vision, language, and action. Inspired by competitive rating systems such as Elo and Glicko, AGI-Elo models each evaluation instance as a “match” between a model and a test sample, simultaneously estimating the competency of the model, the difficulty of the sample and the mastery gap to an oracle.

2.Cross-modal Generality: AGI-Elo applies successfully across six diverse tasks, spanning vision, language, and motion planning. Demonstrates flexibility in handling binary, multiclass, and regression settings with appropriate score normalization.

3.The paper also advances a broader vision for how we assess progress toward general intelligence. By producing interpretable scores that reflect both model skill and task difficulty, AGI-Elo facilitates a richer understanding of AI capabilities and limitations.

summary.value:
This paper introduces a unified rating system that measures the relative difficulty of test samples and the performance of models.
Inspired by the desirable properties of rating systems, the proposed method is formulated as a competitive framework in which test samples and models compete against each other. In this setup, samples that many models fail to predict correctly receive higher ranks, while models that perform well on more challenging samples are also ranked higher.
The authors present extensive experimental results that effectively validate the proposed system.

strengths_contributions.value:
The idea of rating test samples and models by having them compete against each other is interesting.
By doing so, the proposed method can evaluate the relative difficulty of test samples and the performance of models in a more fine-grained way simultaneously.

The experimental results show that the proposed method allows for fine-grained analysis of dataset difficulty and the status of models from the perspective of a specific dataset.
The reliability analysis based on consistency and predictive accuracy demonstrate that the proposed method is consistent with the original task-specific metric and has significant predictive accuracy.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
One possible concern with the proposed method is that the effectiveness and outcomes of the rating system may heavily depend on the number and quality of model agents participating in the competition.
If only a few models are used, the evaluation of sample-wise difficulty may be inaccurate, and the results could vary significantly depending on the number of participating models.
Moreover, if some models perform significantly better than the others, the ratings may be skewed, leading to unreliable outcomes.
A more thorough analysis of these issues would strengthen the paper and make the proposed method more convincing.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value:
The authors' rebuttal has fully addressed the concerns regarding the influence of the number and power of agents on the proposed ranking system.
Considering the method's novelty and effectiveness, I have decided to raise my initial rating to 'accept'.

summary.value: This paper proposes AGI-Elo, a unified rating system that jointly models the difficulty of individual test cases and is designed for matches between heterogeneous agents across vision, language, and action domains to evaluate Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). AGI-Elo can capture both the long-tail distribution of real-world challenges and the competency gap between current models and full task mastery. Experimental results are evaluated across six datasets, validating generalizability and robustness and demonstrating the proposed framework’s predictive accuracy.

strengths_contributions.value:
- This paper is generally well-written and is clear to understand the important aspects.
- The experimental contributions of this paper are significant, with extensive evaluation across different datasets, hyperparameter settings, and ablation studies.
- Besides detailed experiments, the authors also propose a novel rating framework to support evaluating and understanding the behaviour of AGI.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The experiments are not really extensive. Specifically, the number of datasets and models is small, with only one per task.
- The proposed framework requires pre-defining some non-trivial hyperparameters such as the initial rating distribution and the rating bin.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
- It seems that the paper is lacking a standard regression task. Can this framework extend to a regression task, such as evaluating monocular depth estimation in the vision domain?
- In the experiment setup, the players (both agents and test cases) are initialized with a rating from a normal distribution with fixed mean and variance (i.e., $\mathcal{N}(1500,350^2)$), where do these numbers come from? How robust of your framework with different means and variances?

final_justification.value: Most of my concerns are addressed. Hence, I keep my original score and lean towards accepting this paper.

title.value: AGI-Elo: How Far Are We From Mastering A Task?

abstract.value: As the field progresses toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), there is a pressing need for more comprehensive and insightful evaluation frameworks that go beyond aggregate performance metrics. This paper introduces a unified rating system that jointly models the difficulty of individual test cases and the competency of AI models (or humans) across vision, language, and action domains. Unlike existing metrics that focus solely on models, our approach allows for fine-grained, difficulty-aware evaluations through competitive interactions between models and tasks, capturing both the long-tail distribution of real-world challenges and the competency gap between current models and full task mastery. We validate the generalizability and robustness of our system through extensive experiments on multiple established datasets and models across distinct AGI domains. The resulting rating distributions offer novel perspectives and interpretable insights into task difficulty, model progression, and the outstanding challenges that remain on the path to achieving full AGI task mastery. We have made our code and results publicly available at https://ss47816.github.io/AGI-Elo/.

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.
